📺 “Navy Medic Abducted by 15-Foot-Tall Praying Mantis Aliens: The Kevin Kammann Story”
🗓️ Published September 19, 2026
🔗 https://t.co/TkgCVkbDhQ
🕵🏻‍♂️ Preston Dennett — UFO Researcher
👤 Kevin Kammann
🗓️ Abduction: 1982, probably during the summer
⛴️ USS San Bernardino (LST-1189)

Kevin Kammann — The Account of an Encounter with “Praying Mantis” Beings

In the documentary “Navy Medic Abducted by 15-Foot-Tall Praying Mantis Aliens: The Kevin Kammann Story,”Preston Dennett reconstructs the extraordinary experience reported by former U.S. Navy corpsman Kevin Lee Kammann. Dennett emphasizes that Kevin said he experienced the encounter consciously and that his memories were not recovered through hypnosis.

Kevin Kammann and Jeff Reich

Kevin Kammann was born in 1954 and grew up in Kankakee, Illinois, with his fraternal twin brother, Kim. After graduating from high school in 1972, he worked at a hospital and developed an interest in medicine. He joined the U.S. Navy on February 28, 1973, and received medical training at Camp Pendleton.

After a break in his service, Kevin returned to the Navy in 1978 and was assigned as a hospital corpsman aboard the USS San Bernardino (LST-1189).

The first person he met aboard the ship was Jeff Reich, a personnel clerk from Gary, Indiana. The two shared a compartment and soon became close friends, even spending some of their leave time together.

After about four years of Navy service together, Jeff made an astonishing revelation. He claimed that he had been in contact with extraterrestrial beings since he was about ten years old. According to Jeff, he had been taken aboard their craft many times, had visited their planet and other places, and could communicate with them mentally.

Kevin was initially extremely skeptical. As a corpsman, he even wondered whether Jeff should undergo a psychiatric evaluation.

Jeff Describes Kevin’s Home — But in the Past

A few days later, Jeff told Kevin that his “friends” had taken him to Kevin’s family home in Kankakee, even though both men were thousands of miles away.

Jeff began describing very specific details of the house. According to Kevin, he knew things he should have had no way of knowing, including a 1966 Ford Galaxie 500, a chocolate milkshake stain on its back seat, the furniture, carpeting, kitchen, Kevin’s bedroom, and even things that had been written on the bedroom walls.

But there was an even stranger aspect to Jeff’s description: he was not describing the house as it existed at that time. He was describing it as it had appeared ten to fifteen years earlier.

The Ford, for example, had been sold in 1970, and much of the furniture and carpeting Jeff described had been gone for more than a decade.

Kevin began wondering whether there might actually be something behind his friend’s claims.

He finally challenged Jeff:

“Okay, then I want to meet your little green friends.”

Jeff said he would ask them.

The Arrival of the Craft

A few days later, Jeff told Kevin that the beings had agreed to give him a ride.

Kevin still assumed his friend was joking. Then, one day shortly before noon, Jeff told him that they had arrived and instructed him to go up on deck.

Kevin went outside and said he saw a gigantic craft hovering near the USS San Bernardino.

He described it as enormously larger than the ship, completely silent and glowing with brilliant colors — red, yellow, green, purple, orange and others. He compared its appearance to an enormous illuminated diamond.

Even stranger was the apparent reaction of the other sailors: nobody seemed to notice it.

Kevin attempted to attract the attention of a ship’s cook named Brooks, who was talking with another sailor named Davis. Kevin said he even grabbed or shook Brooks’s arm and pointed toward the enormous object, but Brooks did not respond.

Then Kevin experienced what he described as a sudden “shift.”

He was no longer standing on the deck.

Aboard the Craft

Kevin said he suddenly found himself physically inside the craft.

The walls appeared solid but seemed to become transparent wherever he looked through them. He could see the ocean below and the USS San Bernardino becoming smaller and smaller.

His immediate thought was that he was now AWOL.

A male voice answered him telepathically:

“No, you’re not. They don’t even know you’re gone.”

Another voice reportedly told him:

“Yes, it is. It’s what you wanted.”

Kevin then looked toward the ship and described something especially difficult for him to understand: he could apparently see himself still standing on the deck, attempting to get Brooks’s attention.

It seemed as though he was somehow in two places at once.

Returning to Kankakee

Kevin felt no acceleration or conventional movement. Instead, the scenery simply changed.

He suddenly recognized Kankakee.

The craft stopped near the bank building where his father worked. Kevin said he could see through the walls of the building, observing its internal structures until he located his father.

They then moved over the church/school where his mother taught. Again, Kevin said he could see through the building and watch his mother teaching.

The beings reportedly told him telepathically that his parents were honorable people and had done a good job raising him.

Once again, however, Kevin had the impression that he was not simply observing the present. The beings appeared capable of showing him events from the past.

Above the Moon

Another sudden shift occurred.

Kevin saw a dark, gray, cratered landscape beneath the craft. At first, he thought he was looking at some kind of military bombing range on Earth.

Then the craft moved over a ridge.

Kevin saw Earth hanging in space.

He described it as appearing about the size of a tennis ball and realized that he was above the Moon.

The experience seemed so impossible that Kevin pinched the back of his hand hard enough to make himself bleed, hoping to leave a physical mark that might prove to him later that the experience had not simply been a dream.

At another point, he said he was taken into the past again and shown his own home. He saw himself as a boy of about twelve, talking with his grandmother, who would later die in 1972.

The Telepathic Conversation

Kevin began asking the beings questions.

He still had not turned around to look directly at them. He heard their responses telepathically, in perfectly understandable English, but described the voices as monotone and almost emotionless.

When Kevin asked where they came from, a kind of three-dimensional star map appeared around him.

He recognized the Solar System and some of its planets. A distant location was then indicated as the beings’ place of origin.

According to Kevin, they told him that they came from approximately six light-years away and that their journey to Earth took about three and a half months.

Kevin said he could neither remember nor reproduce the name of their planet or species because the sounds were completely unfamiliar to him.

The beings also claimed to understand all human languages and dialects, including languages that had been extinct for thousands of years.

Why They Were Observing Humanity

Kevin asked why they were on Earth.

According to his account, the beings said they had been here for a very long time and were primarily here to observe.

They said they did not interfere with humanity’s religions or politics.

At the same time, however, Kevin said they told him that they interacted with the U.S. government and other major governments around the world. They also reportedly mentioned four other species that interacted with human governments.

Kevin further recalled being told that the Roswell crash was real and that these beings were capable of cloaking themselves.

These statements are part of what Kevin said he was told during the encounter.

Nuclear Weapons and the “Countdown Clock”

One of the most important subjects of the conversation concerned atomic weapons.

According to Kevin, the beings explained that when humanity developed and began testing nuclear weapons in 1945, they and other extraterrestrial species began paying much closer attention to humans.

They reportedly told him that the explosion of the atomic bomb had started a:

“countdown clock.”

They did not clearly explain what the phrase meant. Kevin nevertheless came away with the impression that it referred to some potentially catastrophic scenario.

Images of Past, Present and Future Disasters

The beings then showed Kevin a series of extraordinarily vivid three-dimensional scenes.

He described seeing mudslides, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes, floods, wars, explosions, destruction and large numbers of people being killed.

Kevin said some of what he was shown belonged to the past, some to the present, and some apparently to the future.

Throughout the display, the beings reportedly repeated:

“Some of what you see has already been. Some of what you see has yet to be. These are things that are going to come. The destiny will be fulfilled.”

Kevin said the scenes did not appear like ordinary images on a screen. They looked completely real, almost as though he were actually present and watching the events unfold.

The Vision of His Motorcycle Accident

Among the images shown to Kevin was one that concerned him personally.

He saw an older version of himself riding a motorcycle. An automobile struck him broadside, throwing him to the ground. Kevin saw himself lying there completely motionless.

At the time, he interpreted the vision as showing him how he would die.

For years afterward, the image remained in the back of his mind.

Then, in 2003, Kevin purchased a 100th Anniversary Harley-Davidson Sportster. He later recalled that he had felt uneasy about buying the motorcycle precisely because of what he had been shown in 1982. But he had always wanted a 100th Anniversary Harley, and when his sister-in-law offered to buy it for him under a payment arrangement that was too good to pass up, he accepted.

Kevin owned the Harley for exactly 14 days.

On the fifteenth day, while returning from his brother’s home, a driver made an illegal U-turn and struck Kevin broadside.

Kevin was thrown from the motorcycle and knocked unconscious.

When he regained consciousness, his lower left leg had been shattered.

He underwent surgery the following day and later described having a metal plate and 11 screws placed in his leg. The recovery was extremely long: Kevin said it took 22 months for the bones to heal, followed by approximately another year on crutches.

When Kevin later discussed the accident with Preston, he explained that he then realized what he believed he had been shown back in 1982.

The beings had not shown him his death. In Kevin’s interpretation, they had shown him the motorcycle accident that would actually happen to him 21 years later.

The parallels deeply affected him: the motorcycle, being struck broadside by a car, losing consciousness, and seeing himself motionless on the ground.

Despite the severity of the accident and the lengthy recovery, Kevin eventually improved enough to consider riding the motorcycle again.

“We’re Not Little and We’re Not Green”

Until this point in the experience, Kevin had still not found the courage to turn around and look directly at the beings communicating with him.

Eventually, he asked what they looked like.

They replied:

“We’re not little and we’re not green.”

They also warned him that their appearance might frighten him.

Kevin finally decided to look.

The Three “Praying Mantis” Beings

Kevin described entering or looking into an extremely bright white area containing panels and devices that seemed strangely primitive compared with the extraordinary technology he had already witnessed.

There were three enormous white throne-like chairs.

The chairs turned toward him.

Sitting in them were three gigantic humanoid beings resembling praying mantises.

One stood up.

Kevin estimated its height at approximately 15 feet, or more than four meters.

He described the beings as having:

milky-white skin;
extremely thin bodies;
extraordinarily long, slender arms and legs;
three claw-like fingers;
enormous heads;
gigantic black eyes, roughly triangular in appearance;
no obvious external ears or conventional nose;
facial structures that reminded him strongly of a praying mantis.

Kevin said their heads were enormously larger than human heads and that their eyes appeared larger than basketballs.

He also described an especially unusual feature: parts of their heads appeared partially transparent, allowing him, he believed, to see internal structures, including their brains and blood flowing inside them.

Despite being terrified by their appearance, Kevin believed he was looking at highly intelligent beings.

The Invitation to Visit Their Planet

One of the beings approached Kevin.

It asked whether he would like to visit their planet.

By this point, Kevin’s curiosity had turned into fear. He felt trapped and declined the invitation.

When the being placed a claw-like hand on his shoulder, Kevin panicked and attempted to fight back.

He then lost consciousness.

Back Aboard the USS San Bernardino

The next thing Kevin remembered was finding himself back inside his compartment aboard the USS San Bernardino, covered in sweat.

Jeff was standing there.

Smiling, he said:

“So, tell me about your ride.”

Kevin became furious.

The experience had terrified him, and his relationship with Jeff effectively ended. Kevin even began wondering whether his former friend might somehow be one of the beings in disguise.

After their time aboard the ship, Kevin would never see Jeff again.

The Mystery of Brooks and Davis

Kevin later attempted to determine what had happened while he believed he had been aboard the craft.

He approached Brooks, the cook whose attention he had tried to attract when the enormous object appeared.

Kevin reminded Brooks of the conversation he had been having with Davis on deck and asked whether he remembered Kevin trying to speak to him.

Brooks’s response shocked him.

Brooks remembered his conversation with Davis but insisted that Kevin had not been there. He denied that Kevin had grabbed or shaken his arm.

Kevin then questioned Davis and received essentially the same response.

This was particularly strange to Kevin because, while aboard the craft, he believed he had looked down and seen himself standing on the deck near Brooks and Davis.

The Disappearance of the Memories

After the encounter, something unusual began happening to Kevin’s memory.

Much of the experience gradually faded.

He knew that something extraordinary had happened. He remembered being taken aboard a UFO and retained the feeling that the encounter had been deeply frightening, but many of the details became inaccessible.

Kevin remained aboard the USS San Bernardino for another two years before leaving military service.

Jeff disappeared from his life.

A Praying Mantis on Television

Several years later, in the late 1980s, Kevin was watching television when a close-up image of a praying mantisappeared on the screen.

According to Kevin, the image triggered an immediate reaction.

The “wall” blocking his memories suddenly collapsed, and within minutes much of the experience came flooding back.

He remembered the invitation, the craft, the journey, the conversations and, most importantly, the beings themselves.

Kevin then faced the opposite problem: he could not stop thinking about the experience.

He decided to tell his family. According to Kevin, his family was understanding and believed him, although he also received ridicule from friends and acquaintances.

Events Kevin Believed He Recognized Later

As the years passed, Kevin continued thinking about the disasters he said had been shown to him.

When major hurricanes and other catastrophes occurred, he sometimes wondered whether they were among the events he had seen aboard the craft.

In 2005, while watching television coverage of a deadly mining disaster, Kevin said he experienced another powerful sense of recognition. He turned to his wife and told her:

“I’ve seen this before. They showed me this on the UFO.”

For Kevin, events such as these, together with his motorcycle accident, reinforced his conviction that the 1982 experience had been real.

He also said that the top of his left hand still carried a faint scar from where he had pinched himself while above the Moon. Later, he noticed marks on his leg that he considered unusual and wondered whether there might have been additional aspects of the encounter that he still could not consciously remember.

Kevin Decides to Tell His Story

Over the years, Kevin became increasingly determined to make his experience public.

He believed that people had a right to hear what he had experienced, regardless of whether they chose to believe him.

Preston Dennett eventually documented Kevin’s case in his book Inside UFOs: True Accounts of Contact and helped bring Kevin’s testimony to a wider audience through interviews and radio appearances. Kevin also appeared on Japanese television and spoke publicly about the encounter.

Dennett personally interviewed Kevin in July 2007.

The documentary includes this extensive interview, allowing Kevin to describe much of the experience in his own words, rather than having the entire story related only through Preston’s narration.

Kevin also emphasized that, as far as he knew, this was his only UFO encounter of this kind and that he had no desire to experience anything like it again.

His twin brother Kim, however, reportedly had anomalous experiences of his own, involving beings described differently, as “Greys.”

Kevin ultimately described the encounter as a life-altering experience. Regardless of how other people reacted to his story, he remained convinced that what had happened to him was real.

One of the lessons he drew from it was expressed in a simple warning:

“Be careful what you ask for because you just might get it.”

Kevin Kammann’s Death

Kevin continued for years to speak about the experience and to express his desire for the story to be known.

Kevin Lee Kammann died on April 8, 2021, at the age of 66.

His testimony survives through the interviews he recorded, Preston Dennett’s work, and the accounts in which Kevin described what he believed happened to him aboard the USS San Bernardino in 1982.

The Major Unresolved Element: Jeff Reich

One of the most important unresolved elements of the entire story remains Jeff Reich.

Jeff is not a secondary character.

He is the person who claimed to have been in contact with these beings since childhood. He is the one who said he had repeatedly traveled aboard their craft and had even visited their planet. He is the one who described Kevin’s childhood home with remarkable accuracy, but as it had existed many years earlier.

Jeff communicated Kevin’s request to meet the beings. Jeff announced that they had arrived. And when Kevin suddenly found himself back in his compartment, Jeff appeared to already know exactly what had happened, asking him:

“So, tell me about your ride.”

An independent account from Jeff would therefore be extremely valuable. It could allow his memories to be compared with Kevin’s testimony and reveal which elements of their accounts matched, which differed, and what Jeff might remember independently about the events.

Preston Dennett has not yet been able to locate Jeff, but he will continue searching for him.

Kevin can no longer participate in such a comparison, but his testimony has been preserved through his recorded interviews and Preston Dennett’s documentation of the case.

text:
You can walk into a Catholic church almost anywhere on earth and know exactly where you are.

You could be in Rome, Poland, Kenya, Mexico, the Philippines, or sitting in a nearly empty parish in Chester County on a Tuesday morning. You may not understand a word being spoken, but you will still recognize the Mass. You will know when to stand, when to kneel, what is happening at the altar, and why everyone came.

That alone is incredible. But then you remember what it took for the Mass to survive.

It was offered in catacombs when Christians had to hide. It was offered in prison camps, during wars, in Irish homes when the faith was persecuted, and in underground churches where being caught could cost people everything. Priests risked their lives to celebrate it. Catholics risked theirs just to be there.

Kings died. Empires collapsed. Borders changed. Whole countries disappeared.

The Mass continued.

And now I get to walk into my church on an ordinary weekday morning and step into the same worship Catholics have carried across centuries.

That is what gets me.

Catholicism is not tied to one country, one culture, one preacher, or one generation. The Church is bigger than all of that.

You can cross an ocean, walk through the doors of a Catholic church, and still know exactly where you are.

Another Yemen Podcast from my favorite podcaster @osamaalqutaibi, with two prominent journalists, @YemenShababNet’s @dubalh and @BelqeesTV’s @AhmadALzurqa, to discuss how the Houthis won on the West Coast.

Ahmed: “We defeated ourselves before Iran defeated us.”

Abdullah: “Iran turned the Houthi militia into a state, while our allies turned us from a state into something resembling a militia.”

Part I.

The podcast asks three connected questions. Why did Mocha and Bab al-Mandab fall? What are the Houthis doing with their gains? And what would have to change for their opponents to recover?

Abdullah and Ahmed do not offer a single explanation for the collapse. They describe a combination of battlefield pressure, divided command, political competition, dependence on outside support, and decisions that were not made when the front was still holding. They also discuss allegations of betrayal and deliberate Saudi inaction. Those allegations are part of the conversation, but neither journalist establishes them as solid facts.

Abdullah draws the distinction at the outset. “We said it was not a handover or betrayal. But it was not normal either. It was incapacity and failure.”

His account begins before the final Houthi breakthrough. He says the West Coast had been under sustained attack for weeks, with missiles and drones inflicting losses that were not fully disclosed. The Houthis initially pressed the northern positions around Hays and Al-Khokha before breaking through at Al-Barh. The loss of Al-Barh junction was followed by the fall of Khalid bin al-Walid camp. Once Houthi forces reached a command-and-control center behind the forward positions, the danger of encirclement spread across the defensive line.

The withdrawals that followed made the collapse look sudden, but Abdullah argues that its causes were much older. “There was incapacity and failure more than betrayal.”

The West Coast @NRFYemen forces had been assembled under @modgovae sponsorship from three main components: southern fighters @SouthArmed @alamalikah, Tihami resistance forces, and Tariq Saleh @tarikyemen's National Resistance. The UAE provided a common authority and much of the organization that allowed these formations to operate together. When it withdrew, the forces remained, but their separate loyalties, command arrangements, and political interests did not disappear.

Abdullah credits the Emiratis with earlier military gains. His criticism is that they moved from building a fighting force to building political influence before the military project was complete. He points to the Southern Transitional Council @STCSouthArabia and the National Resistance Political Bureau @P_B_N_R as examples of political ambitions overtaking military priorities. “Rushing the transition from military work to political work ruined both,” he says.

Ahmed is equally critical of what happened after the UAE’s departure. He argues that the Houthi attack was foreseeable, yet the government, Tariq Saleh, and Saudi Arabia @modgovksa failed to prepare a coordinated defense. The Taiz and West Coast fronts were connected geographically but divided operationally. Forces holding positions around Jabal Habashi and other areas answered to different commands from those farther west.

The claim that the armed forces @YemenMOD had been unified does not convince him. “Perhaps on paper. Administratively, they were integrated. Operationally, there was a very serious failure.”

That is one of the clearest explanations in the discussion. The problem was not simply whether there were enough brigades or enough fighters. It was whether anyone could direct them as a single force when the Houthis attacked. 

Ahmed raises allegations about personnel records, undisclosed military facilities, and the deterioration of trust between Saudi officers and Tariq Saleh. 

Abdullah describes the Houthis concentrating fighters and firepower against weak points along an extended defensive line. He says Houthi drones targeted artillery crews and supporting Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS) units, weakening the infantry’s ability to hold its positions. Abdullah also argues that Saudi air cover was largely absent during crucial periods. Ahmed agrees that air support mattered but insists that its absence cannot explain away the failures of preparation and command.

The discussion then turns to the allegation that Saudi Arabia deliberately allowed the West Coast to fall. The journalists consider whether Riyadh distrusted Tariq because of his Emirati ties and whether Saudi decision-makers wanted to reduce his military independence. Ahmed raises a further theory: that a Houthi advance to Bab al-Mandab might force the international community to confront the group and shift some of the burden away from Saudi Arabia.

Abdullah places more emphasis on indecision and failure. “If Saudi Arabia had been serious about preventing Mocha’s fall, it could have done so with its own capabilities, without American intervention,” he argues. That is his assessment of what Saudi Arabia could have done, not proof that intervention would necessarily have changed the outcome.

The journalists are particularly angry about what happened to the men left behind. They describe fighters stranded during the withdrawal, personnel on the islands without adequate evacuation arrangements, and soldiers who were captured or abandoned. They accuse the government and military leadership of failing to take responsibility for those who had fought under their command.

Ahmed asks where the operations room was and who was responsible for the men left exposed. He argues that leaders were preoccupied with explaining the defeat instead of accounting for their forces and rebuilding them. In his telling, the loss cannot be assigned to Tariq alone. Responsibility extends to the government and the coalition because all had a role in the military structure that collapsed.

The podcast also discusses large numbers of dead, captured, and displaced people. These figures are estimates given during the conversation rather than independently established totals. Abdullah describes the effect on Tihami communities whose members had fought for years and on families forced to flee yet again. The human consequences make the debate about command and responsibility more than an argument between political factions.

The first part of the conversation ultimately challenges the idea that the fall of Mocha can be explained by one dramatic moment. The Houthi breakthrough mattered, but the journalists argue that the military system had been weakened by years of divided authority and unfinished institution-building. The retreat revealed those weaknesses all at once.

Part II. 

The second part of the conversation turns from the collapse to the territory the Houthis have gained. Abdullah describes a coastal strip running through Hays, Al-Khokha, Mocha, and Dhubab toward Bab al-Mandab. He says the Houthis reached the strait and moved onto islands, including Perim, also known as Mayyun. His description is a claim about the battlefield at the time of the recording, not an independently verified map of control.

Abdullah is careful about the Kahbub mountains, which overlook the strait from the landward side. He says the Houthis are fighting the Southern Giants Brigades there and have not secured the entire area. “It is still a contested area, with advances and retreats between them and the government forces,” he explains. Abdullah considers the heights more consequential than simply occupying exposed coastal ground because of the military leverage they could provide over the passage. 

He also cautions against confusing a dramatic territorial announcement with the completion of a military operation. Abdullah describes the initial Houthi presence in parts of the newly captured territory as relatively light and suggests that publicity surrounding the advance may have run ahead of consolidation. His concern is what happens if the Houthis are given time to entrench themselves.

The discussion then widens to Taiz and Ma'rib. Abdullah believes the Houthis will first try to secure their gains around Mocha and Bab al-Mandab. He then describes possible pressure eastward from Kahbub toward Al-Turbah and the routes serving Taiz, alongside pressure toward the Safer oil facilities in Ma'rib. These are the objectives he anticipates, not confirmed plans. His argument is that the West Coast cannot be understood in isolation from the other fronts.

Ahmed makes the same point through the contrast in command structures. He says the Houthis have “one operations room, one decision, one movement,” allowing them to apply pressure from Taiz to Al-Bayda while their opponents remain divided. He also argues that the Houthis benefit from Iranian military support and from their opponents' inability to build an equally coherent force. His criticism is directed as much at the government and its allies as at the Houthis themselves.

One of the sharpest exchanges comes when the journalists compare the two sides' military development. Abdullah says, “Iran turned the Houthi militia into a state, while our allies turned us from a state into something resembling a militia.” It is a deliberately stark criticism of the way outside powers have supported competing Yemeni formations. He argues that the Houthis have developed missiles and drones while government-aligned forces have remained constrained by decisions made in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.

The conversation also examines the Houthis' attempt to reassure foreign governments after reaching Bab al-Mandab. The speakers discuss statements suggesting that navigation would remain open and that the Houthis' immediate dispute was with Saudi Arabia. Abdullah compares this approach to the group's earlier assurances to tribes in Amran, arguing that limited promises can help a force consolidate control before its position changes. He sums up his skepticism in one sentence. “Whoever can permit passage can also prevent it.”

The podcast does not establish that the Houthis have made a secret deal with Washington or any other government. The journalists discuss reported communications and speculate about what the Houthis may be offering in exchange for international restraint. They also consider whether pressure at Bab al-Mandab is connected to Iran's confrontation with the United States around the Strait of Hormuz. Those are interpretations of regional strategy, not demonstrated agreements.

For Abdullah, the broader cost is that each territorial gain makes the next confrontation harder. “Every time the Houthis take a commanding or strategic area, their appetite grows, and they begin working on the next area,” he argues. He says recapturing lost territory is possible but becomes more costly the longer the Houthis are allowed to consolidate it.

Ahmed also worries about the psychological effect of the defeat. The idea that the Houthis cannot be beaten becomes stronger with each collapse, while accusations of betrayal spread among the forces opposing them. The journalists connect this loss of confidence to a much wider failure of government. They describe unpaid salaries, poor treatment of displaced families, and armed formations organized around increasingly narrow regional identities. In their account, these divisions undermine the very idea of a national army.

Part III. 

That leads naturally to the final question. What would have to change?

The journalists agree that another round of recruitment or another collection of brigades would not, by itself, address the problem. They argue that the government needs a clear political decision, an effective command structure, reliable support, and an end to the competition between military factions. Ahmed puts it simply. “The problem is not the men. The problem is the political decision, the management of the battle, and the clarity of the vision.”

They disagree, however, over how quickly lost territory could be recovered. Abdullah argues that the West Coast could be retaken if there were a genuine decision, effective air support, professional management, and a reorganized force. But he also warns against promises of an immediate march on Sana'a. “Anyone who tells you we are ready to liberate Sana'a is lying,” he says. He describes the available forces as exhausted and demoralized, requiring time to rebuild their capabilities and confidence.

The disagreement is important because the podcast is not simply a call for an immediate offensive. Its speakers recognize the damage caused by the retreat. Abdullah recounts seeing a video of a fighter who apologized to the people of Al-Khokha for withdrawing. He contrasts that individual apology with the absence of accountability from senior officials. His point is that a soldier who lost his position showed a sense of responsibility that he believes was missing among the people who directed the war.

Ahmed argues that the leadership itself must change if the government wants to restore confidence. He calls for officials, commanders, and security institutions to operate from inside Yemen rather than remaining abroad. Ahmed also wants an end to political quota-sharing and a clearer division of responsibility between political leaders, military professionals, and government institutions. He asks how people can trust promises about the future when the government cannot provide a convincing answer about the present.

The discussion repeatedly returns to the danger of fighting disconnected battles without an overarching political objective. Ahmed criticizes the pattern of sending men to capture individual hilltops only to order them to withdraw shortly afterward. He argues that military decisions should be made by professionals and that the government must consider the people displaced by its operations. 

The journalists also question whether Saudi Arabia has a clear long-term vision for Yemen. Ahmed asks whether Riyadh sees Yemen as part of its strategic security and therefore needs a strong Yemeni state, or whether it sees the country primarily as a sphere of influence. He argues that the current leadership arrangements have failed to produce a functioning state. Abdullah similarly insists that Yemeni and Saudi interests should be treated as shared interests, not as favors one side grants the other.

Their discussion of the United States and other regional powers is less certain. Abdullah predicts a wider confrontation between Washington and Tehran after the November mid-term elections, while Ahmed considers the possibility of international involvement over maritime security. These are their forecasts, not established future events. Both speakers nevertheless question the assumption that Yemen's government can wait for foreign intervention to solve its problems.

The final minutes bring the conversation back to responsibility. Ahmed says Yemen has experienced enough improvisation, fragmented decisions, and costly mistakes. He argues that political leaders should make political decisions, military experts should manage military affairs, and officials should be accountable for the consequences. Ahmed closes with a line that captures his interpretation of the entire war. “We defeated ourselves before Iran defeated us.”

That is the central argument running through the episode. Abdullah and Ahmed see the Houthi victory on the West Coast as a military success made possible by the failures of their opponents. They disagree on some details and speculate about the calculations of foreign governments, but both return to the same unresolved problem. The forces that lost Mocha were never made into a unified, accountable institution capable of fighting independently of their sponsors. Until that problem is addressed, the podcast argues, recovering territory and holding it are two very different challenges.
